newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chinese leader visits Tolstoy estate in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Chinese leader visits Tolstoy estate in Russia.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin, winding up a five-day visit to Russia, took a break from talks on Friday to visit the home of 19th-century writer and philosopher Leo Tolstoy.

Jiang, a known admirer of Tolstoy and a fluent Russian speaker, paid his respects to the autor of "War and Peace" by visiting the writer's Yasnaya Polyana estate about 200 km (125 miles) south of Moscow.

"Tolstoy's works and thoughts belong to Russia and to the whole world as well," said the 70-year-old leader, who once advised young Chinese to avoid decadent Western literature and read Tolstoy's writings and classical Chinese books instead.

Tolstoy's literary talents and his philosophy denouncing violence, official religion and the hypocrisy of the autocratic monarchy, turned Yasnaya Polyana in the late 19th century into a mecca for liberal Russian intellectuals.
Jiang, accompanied by his official entourage, began his Tolstoyan pilgrimage at the writer's home and ended at his grave.

Jiang, who carefully avoided anything which could draghim into Russian politics during his visit, was shown around by a bitter foe of President Boris Yeltsin, Tula regional governor Vasily Starodubtsev, who spent months in prison in 1991 for his part in a hardline coup against Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.

Jiang's visit to Yasnaya Polyana formally ended his visit, highlighted by a joint political declaration with Moscow and a pact on troop reductions along the former Soviet-Chinese border struck with Russia, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan.
The declaration, sighed by Jiang and Yeltsin on Wednesday, outlined their vision of the post-Cold War world and voiced opposition to claims by any country for world leadership.

"No country should seek hegemony, practise power politics or monopolise international affairs," said the declaration. It did not mention any specific country but clearly had the United States in mind.
The United States on Thursday denied Washington sought "domination or a unipolar world" but asserted that the U.S. wielded a special power and influence around the globe.

"Power and influence in the world are governed by interests, by economic power, military power, political influence and values," the State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters in Washington.

"I think it's very clear that the only country in the world that has all those things together and moving forward is the United States. That does not mean that we seek any kind of domination or a unipolar world."

On Thursday Yeltsin and Jiang joined the presidents of Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan in signing the troop reduction pact envisaging cuts of forces along the 7,500-km (4,700-mile) frontier, scene of bloody clashes in 1969.
Moscow and Beijing see the treaty and the declaration as part of a new relationship of "partnership aimed at strategic cooperation in the 21st century," but both sides rule out a closer union.

"We have tried alliance and we have tried confrontation," said Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, referring to the Soviet-Chinese alliance of the 1950s which collapsed into more than two decades of hostility.
"Both did not work and now we must find something else," he said on Thursday. "Our relations are not confrontational but they are not an alliance as well."
Jiang returns to China on Saturday.
